story: Outer space has a distinct smell, described by astronauts returning from spacewalks as a mix of seared steak, hot metal, burnt cakes, spent gunpowder, and welding fumes. Because space is a near-perfect vacuum, no one has ever directly smelled the void itself, as there is no air to carry odor molecules to a human nose. Instead, the phenomenon occurs when astronauts return to the airlock and pressurize the cabin with fresh oxygen. This oxygen reacts with reactive particles like atomic oxygen and ozone that cling to the exterior of spacesuits during low Earth orbit operations. To help astronauts prepare for these unexpected sensory experiences, NASA even commissioned a fragrance chemist to recreate the scent on Earth.
angle: Space actually has a distinct smell resembling seared steak and welding fumes, but you can only smell it after coming back inside.
disputed: Whether the smell is caused primarily by atomic oxygen reacting with cabin air or by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons from dying stars; scripts should note that scientists have competing theories for the exact chemical origin.
